title: Quantifier Negation
short: ¬∀x Fx is equivalent to ∃x ¬Fx, and ¬∃x Fx to ∀x ¬Fx: moving a negation across a quantifier flips ∀ and ∃.
trouble: The scope of negation: learners write ¬∀x Fx as ∀x ¬Fx ("not everything is F" is not "nothing is F").

blocks.html: A negation in front of a quantifier can be moved inside, switching the quantifier, much as De Morgan moves a negation through $\land$ and $\lor$ (De Morgan's Laws). This makes negated quantified sentences easy to read and to use in proofs. It builds on Translating Harder Quantified Sentences.

head: Form
Equivalent form
In words
rows: not everything is $F$ = something is not $F$
something is $F$ = not everything is not $F$

blocks.html:
Moving a $
eg$ across a quantifier switches it: $
eg  orall x Fx$ becomes $\exists x
eg Fx$, and $
eg \exists x Fx$ becomes $ orall x
eg Fx$, whatever formula stands in place of $Fx$. Then keep moving the $
eg$ inward with the rules you know (DM, and $
eg (p 	o q)$ as $p \land 
eg q$).

"Not everything is red" is true exactly when there is at least one thing that is not red: a counterexample. "Nothing is red" is true exactly when each thing fails to be red. In a finite world, $\forall$ is a long conjunction (a is $F$ and b is $F$ and …) and $\exists$ a long disjunction, so quantifier negation is De Morgan's law stretched over the whole domain.

blocks.title: Not all
blocks.q: Rewrite $\neg \forall x(Cx \to Rx)$ with no $\neg$ in front of a quantifier.
steps: A negated conditional is its antecedent and the negated consequent: $Cx \land \neg Rx$.
blocks.a: $\exists x(Cx \land \neg Rx)$: some circle is not red.

blocks.title: In English
blocks.q: What does $\neg \forall x(Px \to Mx)$ say, with $P$: pets and $M$: mammals?
steps: Not every pet is a mammal.
QN: some pet is not a mammal.

blocks.html:
Moving the negation without switching the quantifier, or applying it to only part of the formula. $
eg  orall x Fx$ is not $ orall x
eg Fx$: "not everything is red" is much weaker than "nothing is red". The scope matters too: in $
eg  orall x Fx 	o Ga$ the $
eg$ covers only $ orall x Fx$. Check the scope first, then switch $ orall$ and $\exists$ as the negation moves.

A handy pattern from these examples: once the negation has moved inside, a universal statement usually ends with an arrow inside it and an existential one with an "and". If your result has $\exists x(\ldots \to \ldots)$ or $\forall x(\ldots \land \ldots)$, look again; it is probably a slip.

In proofs, QN is a rule of replacement: it may be used on any part of a line, in either direction. It is often the first step when a premise begins with a negation, because the instantiation rules of the next unit need a quantifier in front.
